policy: Selected editorial relationships, not automatic proof or equivalence. All navigation links remain separately available.

edges.why: The guide uses repair to connect historical warning with present action.
The First Beast inquiry applies the general judgment of domination to a specific identification.
The procurement case asks who defines acceptable information; the robot-religion proposal asks what moral alignment should serve.
The repair framework supplies a constructive standard against which the moral use of authority can be judged.
A theological identification is not the same object as a dated prediction about an outcome.
A personal standard can become a community practice when institutions preserve the ability to correct behavior.
Coherence with human flourishing is distinguished from uniform obedience to an authority.
The constructive theology does not require the proposed genealogy of post-catastrophe literature to have been proved.
Repair asks what can be done while the destructive mechanisms proposed in a forecast remain risks.
An early sayings tradition and a later response to Temple destruction are different possible layers, not one undifferentiated date.
The identity of a historical teacher and the effect of an inward representation are separate claims.
Both inquiries distinguish inherited teaching from a later community's claim to institutional continuity.
The transmission of worship, a volcanic Sinai and the Thera/Ahmose chronology are separable proposals.
Evidence of a divine name crossing a boundary motivates a comparison without proving identical religious institutions.
The register preserves original wording and date basis separately from any later outcome assessment.
The inward representation of Christ is a concrete example of the wider cognitive-spiritual comparison.
Practice concerns the repeated use of an orientation, not only acceptance of a proposition.
Alignment must remain answerable to welfare and truth rather than allowing sacred language to insulate domination.
The comparative method separates canon, sacred place and institutional claims rather than treating shared inheritance as identical religion.
The Teacher inquiry tests whether continuities of message, institution and identity track one another or diverge.
Historical inheritance becomes an inward representation; criticism of the representation is not automatically denial of its referent.
The movement of a name is a concrete case of a boundary crossing that does not establish complete institutional continuity.
The historical identification is one strand inside a larger comparison of teaching, transmission and later interpretations.
The source asks how overlapping portrayals can be used to reconstruct semantic distinctions and inward meaning.
An early teacher tradition and a later literary response to loss can occupy separate layers without proving a direct genealogy.
Explicit scholarly acknowledgments are retained separately from AI-introduced names and new editorial sources.
The June comparison and October earlier-founder reconstruction can be inspected without silently merging their chronologies.
An inward moral model must be able to challenge the person's immediate desire rather than merely justify it.
The priority of a higher moral standard informs the critique of self-authorizing power while leaving individual factual premises checkable.
Repair requires the actor to be correctable, not merely successful at enforcing a preferred outcome.
A teaching system that equates God's will with an operator's commands would fail this proposed moral distinction.
Changing a canon changes which narratives confer authority, but no shorter canon is assumed to settle all moral questions.
The conduct-based judgment is developed through specific scriptural arguments, including mixed cases.
A claim to act for God requires moral examination; sacred status is not the conclusion of that examination.
Justice and accountable care supply a constructive contrast to the religious legitimation of harm.
Explaining a representation does not itself establish or eliminate the existence of what it represents.
Practiced orientation and emotional experience are related to metaphysical belief without being substituted for proof of it.
The teacher's own understanding of God and correction becomes part of what is transmitted to a future conscious participant.
The broader source comparison is one application of the proposed semantic reconstruction method.
A vivid model is not enough; the will comparison asks whether the model can correct self-interest.
Future conscious machines raise the opening inheritance question again: what is transmitted, and by what authority?
Sustained orientation is connected to concrete repair rather than compulsory cheerfulness or denial of danger.
The proposed book begins with rival claims to shared inheritance rather than treating the wiki as an alphabetical manuscript.
Chapter routes are separated from the concrete research and author-review tasks still required.
A visualization preserves the distinction between proposed dates, material evidence and relative textual constraints.
Named debts supply provenance for the investigation without making every later extension a claim endorsed by that author.
The passage comparison carries out the requested Melchizedek sub-investigation without replacing the broader Teacher, Thomas and Gnostic reconstruction.
Shared priestly language is relevant to the reconstruction but does not by itself establish the identity or genealogy of a historical teacher.
Different texts can retain a recognizable priestly figure while changing how the figure authorizes a community.
Release from captivity motivates a philosophical comparison with repair; thematic usefulness is not proof of an uninterrupted genealogy.
The source of legitimate authority and its relationship to an agent's desires remain separate questions.
Coverage records identify actual article links and selected anchors, not a speculative count of sources already read.
The deliverable sequence points to chapter routes without declaring the manuscript completed.
The interval comparison examines a missing chronological constraint and recovers the author's explicit famine-versus-narration qualification.
Daniel connects deliverance and sanctuary restoration, but its event assignments must not be inferred from numerical proximity alone.
The source atlas preserves a proposed institutional reconstruction rather than replacing it with thematic similarity.
The completed first passage comparison is an available component of the larger transmission investigation.
Textual survival, institutional continuity and moral fidelity are distinct dimensions of an inheritance.
Stable source and challenge IDs can support an XR consumer without duplicating or shortening the full arguments.
Trails point to existing chapter routes, not claims that the book or headset experience is complete.
An AI restatement mismatch or invalid inference is documented as an argument outcome, not counted as new archaeological evidence.

anchors.why: The author corrects the reduction of historical catastrophe to a purely inward interpretation.
The author explicitly accepts the name Apocalyptic Repair Theology.
The author connects maximal coherence with God, creation and humanity rather than treating these as competing goals.
The earlier-Teacher dates and identity proposal are stated together.
The author explains the later Peter and James as namesakes or descendants and proposes community continuity.
The author asks for prior research and proposed Egyptian/Ethiopian transmission connections.
The author explicitly asks about Melchizedek across the New Testament, Qumran and Gnostic material.
The author asks how Davidic and Zadokite lines relate to the Melchizedek question.
The author explicitly distinguishes a non-selective famine from a proposed later firstborn narration.
The author states the conquest-before-catastrophe order with illustrative dates.
The author distinguishes an object date from the beginning of the reign.
The author proposes a split and later reunion of communities, not only thematic resemblance.
The author proposes succession, descendants and repeated names as a continuity mechanism.
The author asks for the non-Gnostic Jewish comparison; the turn also contains quoted prior context.
Layered instruction and later accounts of inner teaching.
Recover semantic distinctions across multiple portrayals rather than choosing one compressed summary.
The strong October chronology and proposed identities.
Later communities and namesakes, together with the Two Spirits comparison.
The requested Melchizedek comparison across bodies of texts.
The author identifies Tabor while discussing Paul and James.
A named book and a wider historical synthesis occur in the same author turn; that does not attribute every claim to the book.
The author asks for a broader interconnection of preservation and transmission settings.
Historical theology is connected to the author's broader cognitive research program.
The recurrent pattern and possible transformation of an individual are considered together.
The argument allows repentance rather than treating an individual's identity as a permanent essence.
The inward example supplies a direction of change.
The source explicitly requests nuanced details, examples, quotations and mixed cases.
God is named Purpose or Telos and related to Super Information Theory.
The author asks for possible objections instead of only agreement.
Human flourishing and coherence with God are not accepted as independent alternative goals.
The inquiry asks for semantic reconstruction across sources.
The bridge to the author's earlier cognitive work is explicit.
The original example of a model of Jesus participating in personal change.
The author specifies self-aware, conscious robots as the setting.
A rejected separation between flourishing and coherence is preserved.
The wider religious comparison becomes an AI-facing teaching project.
The relation of faith, vibration, belief and violence is introduced.
The ethical comparison also appears in a lyrical formulation; it is not empirical measurement.
